Skimpy means too little of something — not enough in size, amount, or coverage. It describes things that fall short of what is needed, expected, or proper. Think of it as the feeling you get when you expected more but received noticeably less.
The Two Main Ways It's Used

1. Skimpy clothing (not enough fabric)

When describing clothes, skimpy means very small and revealing — the garment covers very little of the body. This is probably the most common use of the word today.

  • A skimpy bikini leaves most of the body uncovered.
  • She wore a skimpy top that barely reached her waist.
  • The costume was so skimpy that the dancer felt exposed on stage.

The idea is that so little fabric was used that the clothing fails to cover what clothing is usually expected to cover. It's not necessarily bad quality — it's just very, very small.

2. Skimpy amounts or efforts (not enough of something)

When describing quantities, meals, work, explanations, or resources, skimpy means inadequate — there is simply not enough of it.

  • The hotel served a skimpy breakfast — just one slice of toast and half a cup of juice.
  • His skimpy excuse didn't convince anyone.
  • The report was skimpy on details; it barely explained anything.
  • The workers were paid a skimpy wage that wasn't enough to live on.
  • After weeks of exercise, she felt cheated by her skimpy results.
The Tone and Feel of the Word

Skimpy is an informal, everyday word. It's the kind of word you'd use in casual conversation, not in a formal essay or legal document.

It almost always carries a slightly negative or critical tone. When someone calls something skimpy, they usually mean it's disappointingly small — something is lacking, something is falling short. There's often a sense that someone cut corners, was cheap, or simply didn't provide enough.

Compare these two sentences:

  • "She wore a small dress." — just a neutral description.
  • "She wore a skimpy dress." — signals that the dress was notably tiny, possibly scandalously so.

The word skimpy adds judgment or surprise to the description. It's not just small — it's noticeably, questionably small.

It's important not to confuse skimpy with just small or thin. A small book is not automatically a skimpy book. Skimpy specifically implies falling below a reasonable standard or expectation. Something is skimpy when you look at it and think, "That's really not enough."

Also, skimpy doesn't mean low quality in itself — it means low quantity or low coverage. A skimpy meal might be made of perfectly good food; there's just not enough of it on your plate.

Close Relatives (Synonyms) and How Skimpy Differs

• Meager — similar meaning (not enough), but more formal and serious in tone. You'd see meager in a newspaper editorial; skimpy in everyday chat.
  • Scanty — almost identical to skimpy, but sounds slightly more old-fashioned.
  • Revealing — only captures the clothing sense (showing a lot of skin), but doesn't carry the "not enough" idea in general.
  • Sparse — means thinly spread out; skimpy focuses more on overall smallness.
  • Bare minimum — a phrase that captures the spirit of skimpy but isn't a single word.

Of all these, skimpy is the most vivid and versatile for everyday, informal use across both clothing and quantity.
Skimpy = noticeably and disappointingly too small or too little — whether it's clothing that barely covers you, food that barely fills you, or an explanation that barely informs you.
